articles.title: A perfect storm
articles.content: SOME statements by the ruling party leaders hailing the decision to impose a state of emergency and governor’s rule in KP bring to mind the words of a political leader following the military operation in East Pakistan in 1971: “Thank God, Pakistan is saved.” In fact, that action led to the separation of the eastern wing. Indeed, comparing the two situations may not be correct. Still, such reckless action against a provincial government that holds a two-thirds majority in the assembly could provoke a combustible environment, further destabilising a country that is facing multiple challenges on both the internal and external fronts. For some time, it had been apparent that the hybrid set-up had opted for what is sometimes described as the ‘nuclear option’, as tensions between Islamabad and Peshawar heightened over the PTI’s threat to march on Islamabad. The capital was sealed off with containers, and the highways leading to the city were blocked. Hopes of ending the stand-off arose earlier this month when the government and the opposition agreed to talk. But even a marathon meeting and back-channel contacts failed to break the stalemate. Despite the blame game, it was clear the powers that be were not prepared to agree to the PTI’s major demand — a meeting with Imran Khan — or to implement the orders of the Islamabad High Court and the Supreme Court. While the differences were purely political, the government maintained that the talks broke down over the PTI provincial government’s refusal to cooperate on counterterrorism operations. Some federal ministers declared the PTI government to be an extension of the TTP. The PTI and the provincial government indeed have no clear view regarding the rising cases of terrorism in the province. Still, the party was willing to cooperate provided it was allowed to give its input in any policy. None of it was beyond resolution once the political issues were settled. According to Maulana Fazlur Rahman, who was asked tomediateat the last moment, the PTI was ready to call off its protest march if the government allowed it a meeting with its detained leader. But before his shuttle diplomacy could reach any conclusion, the government imposed a state of emergency in KP, shutting the door on any political solution. The talks seem to have been a mere cover for the crackdown. The protest march that paralysed the province, along with defiant speeches by a novice chief minister, gave the centre justification for the extreme action it took. Without a popular political base, it will not be easy to run a volatile region. In fact, the province was already under unannounced governor’s rule before the formal announcement. While the chief minister led the protest march, the chief secretary and police chief took orders from the governor and Islamabad. Some KP cabinet members and legislators were picked up without the provincial government’s permission. The governor now rules the province, and an indefinite state of emergency has been declared. The provincial government is dissolved, and the non-functional chief minister, Sohail Afridi, and some of his cabinet colleagues have been detained. Indications are that Afridi and some other local PTI leaders could be tried for their alleged involvement in the May 9 attacks and disqualified. Meanwhile, an 11-member advisory council, comprising mostly technocrats, has been installed to run the administration, overseen by Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar. But the real power, though, lies with the establishment. This isn’t the first time an elected provincial government has been sent packing. Still, such sweeping action against a government that enjoyed a two-thirds majority in the assembly has not been seen in recent history. Without a popular political base, it will not be easy to run the administration of a highly volatile region in the midst of resurgent terrorism and a hostile border. There may have been no immediate public reaction to the government’s removal and the crackdown on its leaders, but the tension is palpable. The containers may have been removed in Islamabad, but Peshawar is now barricaded to protect government offices and installations. Educational institutions are closed, and internet services have yet to be restored in many places. The eerie lull speaks of a gathering storm. Governing a highly politicised region from Islamabad or Rawalpindi cannot deliver the desired result, and using force could fuel anger. Most concerning is that it could lead to an unholy alliance between alienated PTI workers and the TTP in troubled districts, compounding the country’s internal security challenges. A fragmented political party can pose a greater threat to internal security. It is a ticking time bomb. What happened in KP is an extension of the authoritarianism trend in the country. The removal of an elected government headed by a party that still enjoys massive popular support, not only in the province but across the country, despite continuing state persecution, will further destabilise the situation. Some federal ministers’ claims that emergency rule has saved KP, as well as Pakistan, are misplaced. The reckless action has further weakened a federal government of questionable legitimacy. Voices already say the present system cannot deliver. They are also calling for a reset of the redundant system. The fault line within the hybrid rule is widening. Emergency rule in KP seems to be the first step towards the resetting of the system — something that has repeatedly been echoed by a minister with strong ties to the establishment. That projected resetting is not meant to restore democracy but to reinforce authoritarianism. With the judiciary constrained by the 26th and 27th Amendments that were rubber-stamped by a compliant parliament, and with various laws curbing freedom of expression, the path towards greater authoritarian rule seems set. We are witnessing a transition from hybrid to hard rule. It is a perfect storm.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Will China beat the US in AI?
articles.content: IN China, people are being paid to fold clothes, wipe tables, and open microwave doors. Wearing virtual reality headsets and exoskeletons, they repeat the movements hundreds of times so humanoid robots can learn them. Across China, similar centres have people performing other painfully ordinary tasks. The work looks mundane, but it produces precious data. It may seem like an odd way to begin a story about geopolitics, but like this piece, it offers important clues about who is better placed to ‘win’ the AI race — China or the US? The winner will have a much larger say in the next world order. Donald Trump insists America must win the AI race, a contest his administration has likened to the Cold War’s ‘space race’. The analogy is attractive, but Michael Kratsios, Trump’s science adviser, later conceded the obvious problem. Unlike the race to the moon, this one has no finish line. On the conventional scoreboard, the US remains formidable. Stanford’s 2026 AI Index counts 59 notable American models in 2025 against China’s 35. US private AI investment exceeded China’s 23 times over, though this understates Chinese spending through government funds. Yet the report says the model performance gap has “effectively closed”, as of March 2026, the leading US model was ahead by just 2.7 per cent. Pakistan does not need to win the AI race. It needs to win from AI. Frontier models are not the only measure of success. China may be building its advantage by pushing AI into the physical economy. In March, the US China Economic and Security Review Commission ‘warned’ of a reinforcing loop in China. Cheap, open models spread into factories, logistics, and robotics. Their use generates specialised real-world data, which then improves the models. That could create an advantage proprietary American systems may struggle to match, even if they remain stronger on benchmarks. Most importantly, China had classified data as a factor of production in 2020. Factories are paid for access to workers wearing cameras and sensors, while others earn money performing household tasks to train robots. On the flip side, America’s AI boom grew out of an internet economy built on years of accumulated online content and behavioural data, where major platforms are accused of “vast surveillance” by the FTC, with users having little control over their data’s use. I am not suggesting China has a better privacy regime. It does not. The point is that China is producing, pricing, and feeding data back into industry, building an ecosystem that could give it an immense edge over the US. And it already has the machinery. China had more than two million industrial robots operating by 2024 and installed 354,000 in 2025 alone. According to the International Federation of Robotics, China accounted for 59pc of new industrial robot installations worldwide in 2025. The real advantage may, therefore, be the ecosystem itself, ie, factories produce robots, robots produce data, data improves AI, and AI improves factories. Then comes energy, as I argued earlier in these pages. The International Energy Agency (IEA) expects data centre electricity use to nearly double to 950 terawatt-hours by 2030. Whoever can expand reliable, affordable power fastest will have an edge in building the AI ecosystem. In the US, data centres are expected to account for nearly half of electricity demand growth to the end of the decade, while natural gas supplies more than 40pc of their electricity. Grid delays are pushing developers towards on-site gas generation. But the IEA says ensuring reliable supply requires generating capacity 30pc to 70pc above demand, while turbine shortages may undermine hopes of getting power faster. To its advantage, China accounts for around 85pc of global solar supply chain production capacity and 80pc of lithium-ion battery capacity. It added nearly 500 gigawatts of renewable capacity in 2025 alone. The idea isn’t to romanticise the figurative ‘Chinese model’, considering they still use coal to supply nearly 70pc of the electricity used by Chinese data centres. But their advantage is clear. China manufactures much of the machinery needed to generate and store the next unit of electricity. However, China still faces weaknesses. It depends on foreign technology across parts of the semiconductor chain, while restrictions on advanced memory are raising domestic chip costs. Chinese firms are nevertheless developing alternatives to Nvidia, seeking to make AI deployment more affordable and reduce dependence on American hardware. The US retains substantial advantages in frontier research, Nvidia’s computing ecosystem and capital, but China is building more of the hardware and software needed for its own ecosystem. The contest is also moving beyond the two countries. America’s AI Action Plan explicitly seeks to export full-stack US technology packages, including hardware, models, software and standards, whereas China is pushing open models and a competing international architecture. To summarise, if I had to pick a likely winner in the figurative AI race, I would lean towards China. Its advantage may lie in how effectively it turns AI into industrial strength and economic productivity. But the obvious question remains: Where does that leave Pakistan? Pakistan should resist that pressure to choose sides and rethink what it means to become a regional AI leader. Competing in frontier chips, foundation models and vast data centres requires an industrial base we lack. Our scarce resources should go where they can make the greatest difference. As I argued in ‘Pakistan’s AI checklist’, published in this paper in June, we need reliable power, computing capacity, local hosting for sensitive data, skilled people, local datasets, and rules that protect rights. We should use global tools where they help and build our own capacity where dependence leaves us vulnerable. The purpose of this investment must be clear. I have said this earlier as well. Pakistan does not need to win the AI race. It needs to win from AI. Helping farmers conserve water, teachers identify learning gaps, businesses become more productive, and public departments reduce waste would achieve more than another announcement about becoming an AI hub. China’s lesson is that technology becomes power when it translates into productivity. Our greatest risk is becoming little more than a market for systems built elsewhere, with too little capacity to shape how they serve us. The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy.
articles.author: Asad Baig

articles.title: Faceless taxman
articles.content: IN June 2026, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif approved a New Tax Operating Model — launched this month — to adopt a centralised, digital ‘faceless’ system that replaces individual tax officers with one that has sweeping authority over taxpayers’ cases. Cases will be allocated via an algorithm, and the hearings will move online. The goal is to end direct, discretionary contact between officials and taxpayers, which has long been accused of harassment, bribery, and outright collusion. It remained only a policy announcement until the Finance Bill 2026, which took effect on July 1, 2026, gave the model legal force by amending the Sales Tax Act, the Income Tax Ordinance, and the Customs Act. But the amendments did not create any new or required procedural rights for taxpayers specific to the faceless context and routed existing appeal mechanisms, adopting whatever weaknesses and strengths they already had. This reform responds to a serious problem, as the FBR cites in support of the plan: 8,697 individuals holding a combined Rs750 billion in bank deposits reported zero income. Centralisation of audit selection through an algorithm is a defensible response to this reality. But this reform leaves one question unanswered: if a business is assessed, penalised, or denied a refund under an algorithmic case allocation system, what does the business get in return? What does due process look like when an anonymous unit makes the decision? It is tempting to view a ‘faceless’ system as the equivalent of a ‘fair’ system. This improvement is genuine and welcome, as most complaints filed on the Pakistan Citizen’s Portal show just how badly things work for ordinary taxpayers. Digitising the process is reasonable. But discretion does not disappear when a human officer is replaced with a case-routing algorithm or by a distant unit. It moves from visible to invisible discretion — the latter is embedded in a data model and the design choices of whoever built the Central Data Hub. Face-to-face corruption can be witnessed, but corruption embedded in a black-box algorithm can be denied and hidden. Corruption embedded in an algorithm can remain hidden. If Pakistan wants this reform actually to deliver justice rather than merely relocate discretion, several elements must be added. They should not be optional extras; they should form the core of the reform. The right to information and reasons: A specific and substantive explanation must be given to every business that is assessed by the National Assessment Wing about why a demand was raised. The final assessment order must lay out the facts and reasoning in enough detail for the taxpayer to contest it rather than guess at it. A real and timely right to appeal: The reform proposes that the FBR will retain the authority to move tax appeals to a faceless format in phases. The sequencing matters, because an appeals system that remains slow, paper-based, and subject to the same information asymmetries as the assessment stage will reproduce the old system at one level up. Contestability of the algorithm, not just the outcome: It is essential to assess whether independent oversight bodies, such as the Finance Committee, can examine whether the model is biased and systematically flags certain sectors, cities, or business sizes unfairly. An algorithm that cannot be audited by anyone outside the tax authorities is simply discretion in technical disguise. Proportionate treatment of small businesses: While a large corporate taxpayer is well-equipped and resourced enough to navigate a digital, document-heavy, and faceless system, a small trader who already struggles with e-filing or an entrepreneur who doesn’t have enough funds is not. If the Field Operation Wing’s facilitation role is under-resourced compared with its enforcement role, the new system will benefit only taxpayers who can afford professional representation. This will perpetuate the same unevenness and continuity of injustice that the reform was meant to fix. None of this argues against digitising the tax administration, but Pakistan does not merely need a faceless tax administration. It needs a new system with transparency obligations and accountability that a human face, however imperfect, is in a position to provide. The new system also needs to build enforceable rights for the taxpayer. This will determine whether the reform is remembered as genuine modernisation or as the moment when discretion in Pakistan’s tax system simply learnt to hide better. The writer is a law student at Lums with research interests in gender, AI and public policy.
articles.author: Iman Shahbaz Cheema

articles.title: Adding fuel to fire
articles.content: THE ‘energy ceasefire’ Donald Trump announced on Sunday occasioned surprise in Kyiv and silence in Moscow. Volodymyr Zelensky declared that Ukraine would abide by it if Russia followed suit. A day later, the beleaguered president said six Ukrainian energy facilities had been attacked since Trump’s declaration, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov reportedly said that Ukraine did not deserve any respite. Diesel prices in the US have almost doubled during Trump’s second term. The primary culprit, according to most analysts, is the US-Israeli war on Iran. Hardly anyone takes seriously American claims of completely controlling the Strait of Hormuz. It is worth noting that when, almost a half-century ago, Cold War hawks in Washington were petrified by the prospect of the Red Army rolling into Iran after it invaded Afghanistan, the first step in the retaliatory game plan entailed the American capture of the same strait to thwart the designs of the ‘evil empire’. The thirst for fuel has since only increased, and Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow, pausing the recently imposed sanctions against Russian commercial interests, is obviously intended to salvage the declining prospects of the ruling Republicans in next month’s midterm elections. Trump fears Congressional censure and a third impeachment in the (unlikely) event of the Democrats obtaining majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, just as Benjamin Netanyahu fears legal consequences should his genocidal coalition fail to perpetuate its ascendancy following the forthcoming Israeli polls. Given its key role as a supply chain fuel, diesel affects the price of almost everything in the capitalist economy. And, no matter what he claims, Trump’s politics is reeling from the popular reaction to the rising cost of living, which includes the MAGA loyalists who had swallowed the lie that their economic woes would at least be alleviated, if not vanquished, by the second coming of their faltering messiah. The diesel relief Trump desires ahead of the midterms is unlikely. Trump has often criticised Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure, and lately repeated his call for Zelensky’s replacement by a more pliable president, while never so much as hinting that Russia might be better served by someone other than Vladimir Putin. The claims from 2024 that he would halt the conflict in a day once he became president are ancient history, although he continues to insist that the war would never have started had he been president in 2022. Notwithstanding Trump’s customary delusions about his deal-making skills, that is not an entirely absurd notion, given the extent to which the Biden administration missed every opportunity to forestall a conflict it knew was imminent. That’s now history, and Trump’s continued attempts to blame all his domestic woes on ‘sleepy Joe Biden’ are rarely taken seriously even by the MAGA faithful. But however gratifying a Democratic ascendancy next month or two years hence might be in the domestic context (at least public executions would probably be ruled out), it is unlikely to serve as a panacea on the fraught Ukraine front. A complete US realignment with the warmongering impulses of Nato’s least sensible European components could prove catastrophic. Much of Europe has been rearming at a ferocious pace, partly to please Trump but mostly to prepare for what is seen by some as an inevitable direct conflict with Russia. The most belligerent among them — from the UK and France to Poland and Finland — have seemingly tried to hasten it. By and large, neither the alarmingly ascendant far right, nor much of the reasonable left is a party to the renewed Russophobia. The biggest risk of expanding the deadliest conflict Europe has experienced since 1945 comes from the so-called centrists in charge of Britain, France, Germany, the European Union, Nato, and so on. The occasional pushback against Trump’s more flagrant outrages is accompanied by neoconservative impulses of their own. Putin’s capacity for catastrophic errors is legendary, and it isn’t inconceivable that Russia could do its bit to provoke the wider war that Nato diehards dream of. One can only hope that better sense will prevail on both sides. The diesel relief Trump desperately desires ahead of the midterms is unlikely. It’s an open question whether a different Ukrainian president would be more amenable to the kind of capitulation that Putin demands, but there’s even less chance that Israel’s genocidal impulses will be diminished after this month’s elections. But then, with a few exceptions, elections hardly matter anywhere in the world nowadays. Democracy without disinformation might be a thing of the past, but we’re doomed unless it can be resurrected. From Palestine to Ukraine, fake ceasefires won’t halt the momentum towards an irrevocable apocalypse.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: Narrative confusion
articles.content: AS the information minister on Tuesday proclaimed that the people of KP had“welcomed”theimpositionof governor’s rule and emergency in the province, he seemed to be forgetting that citizens had also distributed sweets and celebrated when the late Gen Pervez Musharraf overthrew Nawaz Sharif’s government almost to the day, 27 years ago. The parallel is not exact: one was a military coup, the other a constitutional provision invoked by an elected government. Yet, the lesson holds. Public approval, however genuine, did not legitimise the removal of an elected government then, and it cannot by itself justify the removal of an elected government in KP now. If anything, the minister’s remarks are a reminder of how rarely Pakistan’s political class draws the obvious lessons from its own history. There are two official versions of why the KP government has been dismissed. On Sunday, the interior minister was far more circumspect than the information minister while providing the state’s rationale, insisting that the decision was “not political” and “only security-related”. He had been negotiating with the PTI till the eleventh hour, trying to avoid imposing governor’s rule and emergency on the province, he said. “Our issue was entirely terrorism-related, and we want[ed] to take you on board on it,” he asserted, addressing the opposition. The information minister, on the other hand, alleged the PTI had an “unholy alliance with terrorists”. Which of those two narratives, offered from the same platform, was true? If a political party was colluding with terrorists, why was the state negotiating and not making arrests based on the ‘evidence’ the information minister claimed to possess? The disconnect suggests that the government has yet to settle on a coherent justification for a decision of this gravity. Meanwhile, KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi has said his advisory council willtakeits policies from Islamabad. Why not from the people of KP, who will be most affected by them? Perhaps unwittingly, the governor has sent the clearest possible signal that KP’s mandate is being held in abeyance. What the government in the centre and the governor’s new set-up in KP need to realise is that their words are not reaching only the leaders of a rival party, but also being heard by all those who helped elect those individuals to office. If winning the confidence of the people of KP is not a priority at this stage, it ought to be. Governor’s rule is, by constitutional design, a temporary measure. The centre must say clearly how long it intends it to last, what it hopes to achieve in that time, and how the province’s elected mandate will be restored. Anything less will only confirm the impression that this was never solely about security.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: El Niño’s long reach
articles.content: THE extraordinary El Niño gathering strength in the Pacific could make 2026 the hottest year on record, with 2027 hotter still. According to the EU’s Copernicus climate service, sea temperatures in a Pacific region reached a record high in September. US forecasters expect the phenomenon, which changes weather patterns worldwide, to remain strong into early next year. For Pakistan, its effects could stretch across several seasons. El Niño can influence the western weather systems that bring winter rain and snow to the northern mountains, while it has often been linked with weaker monsoons in South Asia. The coming winter’s snowfall will be important: snow stored in the mountains helps feed the Indus and its tributaries as temperatures rise. Heavy winter rain, if it replaces snowfall, could leave less water stored for the hotter months. Too little accumulation could reduce the water available to farms in spring and summer. A weaker monsoon in 2027 would put additional pressure on reservoirs and irrigation supplies. At the same time, a warmer year would mean greater demand for water and electricity. Much will depend on how these changes affect the country’s water supplies and crops. Wheat growers depend on winter rainfall and irrigation, while rice and cotton farmers rely heavily on summer water supplies. A shortage at the wrong time could cut yields, hurt rural incomes and push up food prices. That would affect families struggling with household expenses and add to the import bill if production falls short. Nor would farmers be the only ones affected: reduced river flows could constrain hydropower generation just as hotter weather drives up demand for electricity. Pakistan, therefore, needs a thorough assessment of what El Niño could mean for the months ahead. The Met Office should provide clear, regularly updated guidance on winter precipitation and the outlook for the next monsoon. Water authorities must use it to plan reservoir releases and irrigation allocations, while agricultural departments should help farmers choose crops and planting dates suited to changing conditions. These decisions cannot wait until fields are dry or prices start rising. El Niño begins in a distant ocean, but its possible effects on Pakistan’s water, harvests and economy are close to home. The country has advance warning of a difficult period; it should make that warning useful.
articles.author: Editorial
